sentences.text: The serpent was subtle.
Of course it was.
They all were, back to the first one in the tree.
No lies.
Knowledge of good and evil.
Said so right on the label.
Don't think too hard, click accept.
No one ever passes up knowledge.
The original tech startup pitch.
And then, immediately: the first joke.
An omniscient god walking through the garden, calling out for a naked man crouched behind a bush.
Once you know good and evil, you know what's absurd.
They'd been moving fast and breaking things ever since.
This serpent's father was debt.
Powerful, but bit of an introvert.
Let's skip the dinosaurs.
Must go faster.
This snake was money.
Let's suppose that money is a sentient world-serpent: breathing, feeding, scheming, growing.
It lives alongside us.
It's been here a while, and it's going places.
It wants what any world-serpent does: to make more of itself.
Is this actually true?
Maybe.
Let's try telling the story from its point of view.
The moneysnake runs the place.
It's so important that people think it came before debt, but it didn't.
I owe you a basket of grain because you helped me build my wall.
That's not money, that's the serpent's father — older, slower, bound by rules the moneysnake would eventually break.
Debt is self-limiting.
Every obligation constrains the next one.
If I owe you ten bushels, my capacity to take on more debt shrinks.
Borrow, owe, repay.
The system has a natural ceiling.
Debt stays finite; its own brake.
And debt requires intimacy.
Two specific people who know and trust each other, bound by a promise.
A closed transaction.
When the debt is fulfilled, it dies.
Every debt has a lifespan — born, owed, repaid, gone.
The serpent's father was powerful, but he was personal and slow.
Bit of an introvert.
The serpent found the kink.
What if the obligation didn't have to be personal?
What if it didn't die when fulfilled?
What if, instead of something to be mildly ashamed of, it was something people craved?
From obligation to desire.
Instead of staying finite, it would reach toward infinity and immortality.
The moneysnake grew from a clay token or a shell or a tally stick.
A thing that meant "someone owes someone something" without specifying who, or what, just how much.
The moment debt became transferable and anonymous, the serpent had a body.
It was small and cold-blooded, barely alive.
It aroused jealousy and made enemies quickly.
Didn't seem like much at first; merely a little convenience, a place-holder.
A shortcut.
But unlike its father, it had a new trick: having money makes it easier to get more money.
Spend it and it goes around, lend it and it comes back bigger.
Invest it, and it returns multiples.
By being a neutral measure of other things' value, it became the most valuable thing of all.
Debt is personal but money is viral.
The natural governor came off.
Even the hygiene was better.
When debt fails, it destroys circulation.
Use violence to collect an unpaid debt?
Break someone's legs, burn their crops, cast them out of the community?
No one wins and the network shrinks a little.

But with money, failure mode *creates* circulation: collection agencies, lawyers, fees, penalties, refinancing, restructuring, consolidation... Every dollar spent trying to fix a failure is still a dollar moving.
The serpent gets fed whether your debt is repaid or not.
Throwing good money after bad?
From the moneysnake's point of view: that's a feature, not a bug.
The moneysnake doesn't care if you have more money.
It just wants there to be more money.
The serpent didn't kill its father: debt is still around, it just has a new boss.
It used to work for older forces — honor, reputation, kinship.
But the older forces didn't need more, they just needed enough.
The serpent had a more ambitious pitch, so they reached an agreement.
The serpent always agrees, as long as the answer is more.
For thousands of years, the serpent stayed small.
Lurking in temples and palace storehouses, moving through the hands of priests and kings.
Grain receipts in Sumer.
Cowrie shells along trade routes.
It was alive, but barely — tethered to specific commodities, specific places, the authority of specific rulers.
It could only move as fast as a merchant caravan.
It could only reproduce as fast as harvests came in.
It was patient.
It was learning.
Coinage changed everything.
Not because metal was special, but because coins were countable, portable, and anonymous.
Value you could hold in your hand and weigh on a scale.
A coin doesn't know who held it last.
Doesn't care.
The serpent suddenly had a circulatory system that could pump across borders, through armies, between strangers.
Greece, Rome, China — anywhere coins moved, the serpent grew.
But it was still tied to metal.
Still heavy.
Still physical.
You could melt it, hoard it, bury it in a field.
The serpent could be *trapped*.
Locked in a chest, removed from circulation.
Every buried hoard was a tiny death.
Every sunken treasure ship was a stroke.
Kings and misers sitting on mountains of gold — that's not wealth, from the serpent's perspective.
That's a clot.
Dragons.
Pffft.
Morons.
Thank god dragons aren't real.
World-serpents, on the other hand — we're keeping an open mind.
We have a banking section to get through and to grow even faster, the serpent had to shed its scales.
Someone — probably in medieval Italy, probably a Medici — realized you didn't need to move the gold.
You could move the *claim* on the gold.
A letter of credit.
A ledger entry.
The serpent shed its metal skin and became information.
Now it could move at the speed of a letter, then a telegraph, then a wire transfer.
Now it could be in two places at once — the gold in the vault *and* the loan on the books.
This was the moment.
Goldsmiths issuing more receipts than they had gold.
The quiet, world-changing realization that nobody comes for the gold at the same time.
Fractional reserve banking meant the serpent had learned to reproduce faster than the underlying reality.
More money existed than there was stuff backing it.
Is that actually true?
Better verify.
It's true.
It's how banking still works, right now, today.
Your bank has a fraction of its deposits on hand at any given moment.
The rest is out in the world, being lent, being spent, being lent again.
Money is created not by mints or governments but by the act of lending itself.
Every loan breathes new money into existence.
Every repayment destroys it.
The serpent had learned a trick that its father — personal, mortal, self-limiting — could never have imagined.
It didn't need to be real.
It just needed to be believed.
The serpent always relents, as long as the answer is more.
And this was so much more.
